tip: 'Achter' means behind: 'achter het huis' = behind the house.
'Vanaf' means from a starting point: 'vanaf de brug' = from the bridge.
'Tijdens' means during: 'tijdens de vergadering' = during the meeting.
Before a plural noun the adjective normally takes -e: 'verse sinaasappelen'.
When introducing people, 'dit' stays singular even before a plural: 'dit zijn mijn buren'.
Next or last plus a time unit needs no preposition: 'volgende maand' = next month.
'Er' is a dummy subject for there is/are and is not translated: 'er staan vijfduizend bomen' (there stand five thousand trees).
Illnesses often use 'hebben' with no article: 'koorts hebben' = to have a fever, literally have fever.
'Genieten' takes 'van' for what you enjoy: 'genieten van de zonsondergang' = to enjoy the sunset.
'Goed' has an irregular superlative: 'beste', not 'goedste', just like English good becomes best.
After 'waarom' the clause sends its verb to the end: 'de reden waarom hij vertrok'.
'Een appeltje te schillen' literally means a little apple to peel, the Dutch way of saying a bone to pick.
'Je/jij' is the informal you for friends and peers, as in 'kun je'; switch to 'u' for strangers, elders, or business.
'Zich bevinden' = to be located; the 'zich' stays with it: 'waar de bushalte zich bevindt'.
After a place noun, 'over' shows motion across: 'de brug over' = across the bridge.
'Overtuigd van' – many Dutch adjectives require a specific preposition: 'bang voor', 'blij met', 'trots op'.
After a number, a unit like 'kilometer' stays singular: 'achttien kilometer', never 'achttien kilometers'.
After 'had', a verb like 'kunnen' keeps its full form: 'had kunnen vermoeden', not 'had gekund'.
'Bang' takes 'voor' where English uses of: 'bang voor onweer' = afraid of a thunderstorm.
To say no or not any before a noun, use 'geen', not 'niet': 'geen kaartjes meer' = no more tickets.
'Elke' means every and is always followed by a singular noun: 'elke maandagochtend'.
'Dank je wel' is informal thanks; switch to 'dank u wel' with people you address as 'u'.
A helper verb like 'kan' pushes the main verb to the end: 'kan het niet alleen doen'.
'Benieuwd' pairs with 'naar', not 'over': 'benieuwd naar het resultaat' = curious about the result.
An adjective before a de-word normally gets -e: 'een sterke smaak', because it is 'de smaak'.
Dutch prefers a posture verb: a flat book 'ligt' (lies) on the table, rather than just is.
Cars and upright things 'staan', not 'liggen': 'de auto staat achter het huis'.
With 'vandaag' first, the verb 'ga' must come second, so the subject follows: 'vandaag ga ik'.
For a state still going on, Dutch uses present tense with 'al': 'zijn al tien jaar getrouwd'.
Units of measure stay singular after a number: 'honderd meter', never 'meters'.
